item.title: Grow with your AI agent skills
item.description:
When I started drafting posts for this blog with an AI assistant, I asked for something short and casual. Reading the first drafts, I found myself wanting another paragraph or two in places. A good example deserves enough room to make sense, and a link to the official reference gives a curious reader somewhere to go next.

That’s the kind of thing I’d put in an agent skill, a set of instructions an AI assistant can reuse for a particular kind of work. The writing skill for these posts can capture what I mean by “casual” and which details deserve room. The next time I write a post, I can start with those preferences and see how they hold up on a different topic.

item.title: Why every student should learn Git
item.description:
I think every student should learn some form of version control. Git is a good place to start, especially if you work with code or plain text. I appreciate it most when something was working yesterday and I can’t remember what I changed. With a few meaningful versions saved, I can compare what I have now with the version that worked. Pro Git’s introduction to version control

The same idea works for writing. Imagine cutting a paragraph from a report, then realizing a week later that it contained the clearest explanation you had. You can pull that paragraph out of an earlier version and keep the rest of your edits. A short message about why you saved a version helps, too. “Reorganize the results around the two main findings” tells you something that a filename like report-final-v3 can’t.

item.title: Why I keep my notes in Markdown and Obsidian
item.description: I like being able to open a note and read it right away. With Markdown, I can see where a section starts, what belongs in a list, and where a link goes, even in a plain text editor. A line starting with ## is a heading. That little bit of structure is enough for most of what I write down. If you’re curious about the syntax, CommonMark has a short tutorial you can open in your browser. CommonMark’s Markdown tutorial

item.title: Why I like keeping a work log
item.description:
The hardest part of switching between projects is often remembering where I left off. A few days later, I might remember that I tried something and that it worked. The part I actually need is what I changed and why I stopped there.

A good log entry can be two sentences. “Lowering the batch size stopped the crash. I still need to see how much slower it runs.” That’s enough to pick up the work without repeating the experiment or rereading a long chat. When I have several things going at once, I find it easier to leave a line like that before switching projects than to reconstruct the whole day later.
